title: She loved much (Luke 7:36–50)
hook: a woman with a reputation washes his feet with her tears at a proud host's dinner

segments.voice: Yesterday, John's question from prison and wisdom's children. Your line was go and tell what you've seen. Did you say your question out loud to someone? Day five hundred twenty-nine.

A dinner party at the house of a Pharisee named Simon. The guests recline on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow, their feet stretched out behind them. Some historians think dinners like this could be semi-public, with people from town standing around the edges to listen. And one of them slips in. Luke calls her "a woman in the city, which was a sinner." He never says what her sin was, and he never gives her name. She's carrying an alabaster jar of perfumed oil. She stands behind Jesus, at his feet. And before she can do whatever she came to do, she starts to cry.

Luke, in the King James words: she "began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment." The room goes quiet. Simon thinks, but doesn't say: if this man were a prophet, he'd know what kind of woman this is. Jesus answers the thought: "Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee." And Simon, politely: "Master, say on." Notice that Jesus speaks to Simon by name, as his host, not as a villain. He tells a little story. Two people owe a moneylender, one five hundred coins, one fifty. Neither can pay, and he forgives them both. "Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?" Simon: "I suppose that he, to whom he forgave most." Then Jesus turns toward the woman, while still talking to Simon: "Seest thou this woman?" That might be the question of the whole story. Simon has seen a reputation. Jesus asks him to see a person. You gave me no water for my feet, Jesus says; she washed them with tears. You gave me no kiss; she hasn't stopped kissing my feet. You didn't anoint my head; she anointed my feet. Then: "Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little." And to her, directly: "Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace." She came in carrying a reputation. She leaves carrying peace.
screen: then, large: `HER SINS, WHICH ARE MANY, ARE FORGIVEN; FOR SHE LOVED MUCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept being forgiven. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've done that you still carry. Not the worst thing, necessarily, just something that still makes you wince. Maybe you've been forgiven for it already, by the person or by God, and you've never quite let it in. Picture yourself at that table, in the woman's place. Hear the words: go in peace. Not you're a good person. Not it didn't matter. Just: forgiven, go in peace. Breathe in, and let it reach you. Breathe out, and set the weight down for these two minutes. Notice what's left when the weight is gone. If you pray, you can hear those words as spoken to you. If you don't, simply practice putting the weight down. The bell holds the time.
Agapao, the Greek word for love behind the phrase she loved much: an unnamed woman at a Pharisee's dinner washes Jesus' feet with her tears, forgiven because she loved so greatly.
Your line: seest thou this woman. Today, when you see someone's reputation before you see them, hear Jesus' question to Simon: seest thou this woman? Look again. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Christians read this story when thinking about confession and forgiveness, and the woman's tears are often remembered as a picture of love and repentance.

original.note: Greek: she loved much. from agapao, to love.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a sinful woman.
what it means: a story about seeing. Simon sees a reputation; Jesus asks him to see a person who loves much because she has been forgiven much.

what a scholar hears: "for she loved much" can sound like love earns forgiveness, but the parable just before points the other way: love is the response to being forgiven. readers still weigh the two.

notes: The woman is unnamed in Luke. Western tradition later identified her with Mary Magdalene; that is left for tomorrow's day and not asserted here.
Reclining at table and onlookers at semi-public meals: common historical reconstruction. Confirm.
